title: Read and execution permissions and approval requirements

opening.headline: When an app is connected, it explains how much AI can do on its own, organized into a structure of read and execution permissions and approvals.
body: Connecting apps like Mail, Calendar, and Drive to AI makes it easier to find files or summarize messages. However, some apps can even perform actions within connected services. If so, it's natural to feel anxious that emails might be sent out or my schedule changed without my permission.

In this lesson, we distinguish between two types of permissions: read and execute, and take a side-by-side look at how ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini handle authorization. At the end, we will explain through examples why the approval methods for sending mail and schedule registration are designed differently, and we will summarize the criteria for judging the approval level appropriate for business risks.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between read/execute permission and approval request
The approval method of the 3rd party connection function can be matched.
You can determine the approval level appropriate for your business risk.

screens.title: How far can AI go if you connect apps?
screens.lead: First, let's look at situations where the connectivity feature is turned on. Read the scene below and think about what makes you uneasy.

visual.alt: A scene with mail, calendar, and drive icons on the left and an AI icon with a question mark on the right.

paragraphs: Connect your app to AI so that AI can find files, summarize documents, and check messages in your connected accounts. As convenient as it is, I wonder what AI can see inside my account.

What concerns me more is the movement. Some apps even perform supported actions on connected services, such as sending messages or creating events. It's a problem if an email goes out or my schedule changes while I'm not looking at it.

This anxiety can be resolved by dividing it into two parts. AI's permissions to only view and change permissions are different, and changing actions usually require an approval step. Today we will check this structure in three services.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which is more difficult to reverse: reading or changing? By the end of class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: To identify anxiety for what it is, let's start by thinking about what to check before clicking allow.

screens.title: before clicking allow
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What do I check before pressing Allow on the permission request screen?
items.answer: The basics are to check which app is making the request, what action is being requested, and whether it can be reversed once executed. It is best to avoid the habit of allowing names just because they are familiar.

items.prompt: Do you think AI can read files that my account doesn't have access to?
items.answer: Following Claude's instructions, the connector inherits each user's permissions in the connected service. AI can't import files or channels that you don't have access to. However, the following screen confirms that this is not the case for all connections.

items.prompt: Who turns on and off the AI connection function used by the company?
items.answer: Even apps that are connected to individuals can often only be used within the policies set by the administrator in a work environment. Remember that personal and administrator settings work in conjunction with each other.

screens.outro: Let's organize the things we want to check into read, execute, and approve.

screens.title: Read and execute permissions
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to see how reading and executing differ and what risks they pose.

visual.alt: An illustration comparing the reading example card and the execution example card left and right.

states.label: read permission
states.body: Reading involves finding, retrieving, and summarizing information from connected accounts. ChatGPT documentation explains that the app lets you find files in services like Google Drive or Slack, summarize documents, and look up messages. Reading does not change anything within the service, so the risk is relatively low. However, if the reading range is wide, sensitive information may be revealed in the summary, so you should check which accounts and folders you are accessing. Claude inherits each user's permissions from connected services, so it can't retrieve material you can't see.

states.label: execute permission
states.body: Execution involves sending a message, creating a schedule, or changing a file within a connected service. Gemini can help edit and manage the content of other apps if the user gives permission, and the ChatGPT document explains that app permissions control when to read information and when to perform actions. Execution is riskier because it changes the state of the service. In particular, actions that affect external services, reveal sensitive information, or are difficult to reverse are subject to further review.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the types of permissions, let's take a side-by-side look at how the three services handle authorization.

screens.title: 3rd party approval method and manager control
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the approval steps and administrator controls of the three services.

tabs.label: ChatGPT
tabs.body: ChatGPT's app permissions are divided into four levels: Always ask asks first, whether before reading or changing information. Allow read actions does not ask for reads, but only before changes. Allow low-risk actions automatically approves low-risk actions, while high-risk actions can be confirmed or rejected. Allow all actions performs supported actions without additional permission and is advised to carry a high risk. This last option is not available in normal account-wide settings. Actions that affect other services or are difficult to reverse, such as sending emails, deleting files, changing access permissions, or making purchases, may be subject to additional review and your request may be denied without an approval screen.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude's connectors allow Claude to access apps and services, retrieve data, and perform actions within connected services. The key is to inherit authority. If you can't access a file, channel, or record from a connected service, you won't be able to import it from Claude. However, custom connectors that use shared credentials will reach everything that those credentials can access. So what credentials you connect with determines the scope of your access.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: The Gemini app may, with your permission, help you edit and manage content in other apps. Additional conditions apply for company or school accounts. You must have the applicable Google Workspace edition and have the Activity setting turned on, which can only be managed by Workspace administrators. It's important to note that the screens and policies are different for personal and professional accounts.

tabs.label: Administrator Control
tabs.body: In an organization, there is a range of tolerance from managers that is separate from individual approval. In ChatGPT's Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces, you can review and change plugin and app installation, app access, and behavior in the administrator console. New plugins and apps are disabled by default in Enterprise·Edu and enabled by default in Business, and administrators can change their availability. Being able to use it and approving personal account connection/operation are separate. No matter how permissive your personal settings are, administrator policies may take precedence, so work accounts should see both tiers together.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed that personal approval and administrator permission work together, let's consider an example.

screens.title: Explanation: Why are email sending, schedule registration, and approval different?
screens.lead: The instructor compares two movements based on the same criteria and explains the process of determining the approval level step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: We connected the mail app and calendar app to AI. AI can now send meeting information emails and register schedules. Can I approve both actions in the same way? The starting point of this case is that this is not the case.

steps.title: Can it be reversed?
steps.body: Registering a schedule means adding an item to your calendar, so if something goes wrong, you can delete or edit it. Once an email has been sent, it is difficult to retrieve it. Even with the same execution permissions, the reversibility is significantly different.

steps.title: Who does it affect?
steps.body: The schedule is largely a change within my domain. The mail reaches an external person. Sending emails is one of those actions that the document says are subject to further review: actions that may affect other services or are difficult to reverse.

steps.title: Recommended approval level
steps.body: When sending emails, the appropriate setting is to check the content each time and then approve it. Schedule registration may be deemed low risk and reviewed for automatic acceptance. However, emails containing sensitive information are checked directly under any setting.

steps.title: View administrator policies together
steps.body: In a work environment, administrator policies may take precedence over personal settings. Even if I try to change it to auto-allow, the organization's policy may block it, and conversely, if the organization does not turn on the connection function, I cannot use it before changing the personal settings.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The approval level is determined by the risk, not the name of the action. The more irreversible and externally impacting an action, the more human approval it requires. Conversely, actions that are easy to reverse and stay within your scope may be worth considering automating.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the principle of approval levels tailored to risk.

screens.title: Match approval levels to risk
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard. Read this while thinking about the tasks you want to automate.

paragraphs: Reading refers to viewing information, and executing refers to changing the state of a service. Reads are relatively low risk but require scope verification, while executions require levels of acceptance based on reversibility and external influences.

Approval is not one layer. There is a level for users to allow or deny each action, and in your organization, the apps and scopes that your administrator has allowed are on top of that. The two layers work together, so you shouldn't rely solely on your personal settings.

When deciding which steps can be automated, look for three things: Is this action reversible? Does it affect external people or other services? Does it contain sensitive information? Start by reviewing your automation with actions that can answer no to all three questions. Conversely, if even one of the above applies, it is safer to leave a human approval step. One method is to start with the most stringent settings at first and expand the range as you gain experience. The scope of automation should be based on acceptable risk, not convenience.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The more irreversible an action is, the more approval it requires. The approval level is determined by the risk, not the name of the action.

glossary.def: Permission to find and retrieve information from connected services.
This is the right to perform actions such as send, create, and replace within the connected service.
This is the step where the user decides to allow or deny before the AI operates.
It is a control device that allows organization administrators to determine which apps can be used and to what extent.

misconceptions.myth: If you connect an app, AI can do anything.
misconceptions.fact: AI operates only within the access rights, app permissions, and administrator policies of connected services. Claude inherits each user's privileges.

misconceptions.myth: Once you allow it, it's safe forever.
misconceptions.fact: Privilege levels can be revisited and changed later. You can adjust your settings on a per-app or per-account basis, so check back regularly.

misconceptions.myth: There is no risk as long as you read it.
misconceptions.fact: Reading doesn't change the content, but sensitive information may be revealed in the summary. You should also check your reading range.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Read and execute are permissions with different risks.
Approval is an overlapping user level and administrator whitelist.
The more irreversible an action is, the more approval it requires.
All three services either inherit authority or leave an approval step.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In my work, which steps can be left automatically and which steps must be checked by me?

checks.q: What most accurately describes the difference between read and execute permission?
options: Reading is finding and summarizing information, and executing is changing something within a connected service.
Read can only be used by administrators, and Run can be used by all users.
Reading is irreversible, execution is always reversible
Read and Execute have different names but the same risk level.
checks.explain: Reading is seeing, and doing is changing things, like sending a message or creating a schedule. Therefore, app permissions are also controlled by distinguishing between reading time and operation time.

wrong.1: Permissions are inherited on a per-user basis or adjusted by administrator policy, and read is not exclusive to administrators.
wrong.2: What is difficult to reverse are usually executable actions such as sending an email.
wrong.3: Execution has external influences and divides approval levels more carefully than reading.

checks.intro: Check for yourself the division of authority you just learned about. Results are not recorded, and commentary appears immediately after you select an option.

checks.q: Match the following actions with the appropriate authorization method:
left: Whether to enable connectivity (Gemini for Business)
right: Since it is reversible, it is considered a low risk and automatic permission is considered.
Workspace administrator must turn on the connection function to use it.
Since it cannot be retrieved, check it every time.
checks.explain: The more difficult it is to revert, the more approval is required, and in a work environment, admin policies work in conjunction with personal settings.
